An exploratory study is presented to estimate the decay lifetime of the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ process using existing experimental data, specifically from LHCb. A straightforward method is used to calculate the lifetime, first considering potential biases in experimental results, and then developing a simple theoretical approach to predict it. The estimated lifetime and associated uncertainty are calculated for two distinct $K^+$ momentum ranges, and it is shown that the lifetime remains relatively consistent across these ranges. The study demonstrates that the decay lifetime is likely longer than 1 picosecond, with a precise value dependent on experimental measurement.

This research paper focuses on the numerical solution of a controlled parabolic equation with random initial conditions. We consider a specific finite difference method for the one-dimensional case and conduct an error analysis to demonstrate its convergence. Additionally, we provide a general framework for the analysis of a similar method applied to a system of equations in multiple dimensions. This work builds on earlier research by J. Liu and Y. Yue, who examined a similar method for a specific type of parabolic equation with random coefficients.

Our in-depth analysis of ultra-high energy cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant fluctuations in the cosmic-ray flux as measured over vast areas of approximately 72 million square kilometers. This conclusion is drawn from observations of cosmic-ray interactions observed by 61 observatories spanning a time frame of 11 years. We calculated the cosmic-ray flux at various scales, starting from small areas of about 10,000 square kilometers and comparing them to the expected values based on larger patterns. Our findings show a significant disparity between observed rates and predicted rates within small areas, particularly for events above 4 EeV, where a notable excess of events was found in certain areas, with a probability of less than 3 in 10,000. We also explored potential influences of local cosmic-ray accelerators, magnetic fields, and neutrino interactions, but concluded that these would have an insignificant impact on our results, with a probability of more than 99.9%. Our research provides a comprehensive understanding of ultra-high energy cosmic-ray fluctuations on a cosmic scale, with implications for the field of high-energy astrophysics and particle physics.

The ATLAS particle detector within the Large Hadron Collider's experimental framework examined the output of proton-proton, lead-lead and proton-lead collisions between 2013 and 2015. By re-examining existing data, a better comprehension was achieved of the output of proton-proton collisions, allowing for more precise calibration of the detector. Additionally, characteristics of the output of lead-lead and proton-lead collisions such as particle multiplicity, the average transverse energy per particle and the nuclear alteration factor were re-determined.

This work explores the fundamentals of quantum mechanics within a noncommutative geometric framework, centered on Lie algebras, and examines both classical and operator approaches to the coordinate commutation relations that these algebras imply. We examine three strategies: one based on an operator representation of the algebra, another rooted in classical statistical mechanics, and a third inspired by an operator treatment of the algebra's classical form. We discuss both the challenges and successes of these strategies in describing standard quantum phenomena, including energy patterns, decay rates, and probability distributions in one- and two-dimensional scenarios.

In evaluating the potential of federated learning, we tested its performance in training a convolutional neural network to classify tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes based on their abundance and type. By simulating a FL environment with a large, diverse data set of 25,000 images, we compared the results of training models in a federated setting to those obtained through centralized learning. The findings showed that models trained in a federated manner were comparable to those trained through centralized learning, with an accuracy of 92% in the private round, indicating that FL is a viable approach for this type of classification.

In this study, a high-speed underwater fiber transmission system utilizing super-dense WDM is demonstrated, reaching data rates of up to 72Gbit/s per channel. However, the system is prone to signal distortion due to the high fiber attenuation and limited splicing capabilities in deep-sea environments, which severely limits data transmission speed. To counter this issue, a decision-feedback equalizer (DFE) is implemented to compensate for signal distortion, but its effectiveness is hindered by burst errors caused by the limited dynamic range of the analog-to-digital converter and poor received signal quality. To address this challenge, this study investigates the incorporation of a minimum mean square error (MMSE) filter within the DFE to mitigate the impact of burst errors. The implementation includes the design of a reconfigurable and energy-efficient DFE-MME ASIC, capable of supporting up to 16 channels with data rates of up to 48Gbit/s per channel, and has been successfully tested in a 120km underwater fiber transmission system. The results show a significant improvement in bit error rates, with some channels achieving error rates below 10^-7. The low power consumption of the ASIC, around 24mW, makes it an energy-efficient solution for underwater fiber transmissions. The study demonstrates the potential for high-speed underwater communications, with data rates of up to 2.4Tbit/s being achievable over a 120km transmission distance. The work has been validated by actual field transmissions.

Temporal convolutional networks have gained popularity in time series forecasting due to their flexibility and efficient use of memory. However, TCN's connection-based convolution method can lead to excessive parameter efficiency, particularly when optimizing real-world datasets. To address this challenge, a new trimming technique called Trimming In Time (PIT) has been developed to efficiently optimize TCN's parameter framework for time series data. By employing a custom trimming strategy, PIT successfully reduces unnecessary parameters generated during convolution, resulting in substantial gains in model efficiency without compromising performance. Experiments conducted on real-world datasets, including M4, prove that PIT achieves a balance between model efficiency and accuracy. A comparative analysis of PIT with existing trimming methods and model architectures, including Graph Attention Networks and WaveNet, reveals that PIT delivers superior performance in terms of both efficiency and accuracy.

This paper establishes that any variety of linear algebras, which includes but is not limited to, nilpotent, solvable, or abelian algebras, necessarily encompasses all varieties of Mal'tsev or Tarski algebras. Consequently, any variety of linear algebras is either minimal or it is extensive and encompasses all varieties of groups. Furthermore, we determine all nilpotent algebras whose laws are in accord with those of some group G, thereby solving problem 3 from "Linear algebras and related structures" (Amsterdam, 2005).

Our study sheds new light on the behavior of transverse flow at unusual angles and its relationship with collision energy. We used data from the ALICE detector at the LHC in two different energy levels, 2.76 and 5.02 TeV. Measurements of the coherent cross-section in heavy-ion collisions allow us to test Perturbative Quantum Chromodynamics predictions at a new scale. Additionally, we investigated the connection between flow fluctuations and collision centralities in three dimensions. Our results demonstrate that initial state longitudinal geometry influences flow direction and intensity.

The concept of correspondence theory for modal logic is a well-established idea, providing a framework for exploring connections between model theoretic and proof theoretic properties of modal logics. Building on correspondence theory, our approach develops a more comprehensive framework that can derive both correspondence results and the efficiency of proof systems, such as cut-free or normalisation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to several modal logics, including their extensions and fragments. Specifically, we obtain correspondence results for (1) basic modal logics, such as KP, BAL, and their extensions, (2) extensions of modal logics with S5, (3) prepositional modalised logic, and (4) the Lewis modal logics of relation algebras. Our approach is also suitable for analysing the relationship between our method and other techniques, such as the original correspondence theory or the double step rule of the Lean Lean Mathematical Assistant.

Data integration, a critical task in data management, involves combining data from multiple sources. This abstraction focuses on integrating tables with at least one common table, assuming certain relationships between the data. It addresses three key challenges in data integration: handling missing information, managing data inconsistencies, and resolving conflicts during the merging process. This research aims to provide methods for handling the three issues mentioned above, including new techniques for correcting data based on specified relationships between the data and existing approaches for the other two issues. Furthermore, this work also offers strategies for merging data, utilizing the methods for handling missing information and data inconsistencies. Three use cases are presented to illustrate the application of these methods in real-world scenarios.

This study presents a novel temporal-variance Poisson autoregressive model called TVPAR($p$,$q$) that generalizes previous count time series models. The TVPAR model incorporates a dynamic variance process linked to its lagged absolute values, enabling the capture of periodically changing variances in time series data. A notable advantage of this model is its transformation into a constant-variance process via a square-function, ultimately facilitating parametric estimation using maximum likelihood estimation. Furthermore, we have derived the theoretical characteristics of the TVPAR model's parameter estimators, including their asymptotic distribution and bias-corrected forms. We have also developed the SAMTVA algorithm for parameter estimation and variable selection in the TVPAR model, leveraging the bridge estimator and cross-validation. In addition, we have investigated the TVPAR model's forecasting performance and its ability to handle variable selection in simulations. Additionally, we have analyzed real-world Poisson time series data using the TVPAR model and present our findings.

We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), an object representation that uses a neural network to predict a pose-invariant descriptor located on an object, enabling robust Grasping, Pose Estimation, and Manipulation tasks. NDFs are designed to be highly versatile and can be created even when training on limited and low-quality data. To guarantee pose-invariance, the descriptor is positioned on a geometric object shape, specifically on the surface of a revolution, making it invariant to rotations. To handle translations and other pose variations, NDFs are trained as a regression task. We demonstrate the effectiveness of NDFs by developing a simple pose estimation algorithm and successfully testing it on various objects and scenes. Code and data are available at: https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~ndf/.

The SiD (SolidaD detector) concept has been a leading idea for the detector suite for future $e^+e^-$ colliders, specifically HLLC (High-Luminosity Large Detector) and CLIC. Given that the HLLC design has been incorporated into the HDiR (Higgs Factory Detector) concept and HLLC's silicon vertex detector proposal has been revised, the original SiD document has become outdated. This presentation revises the original SiD concept, aligning it with the revised HLLC vertex detector and R&D findings from the SiD's development period.

We performed the first in-depth analysis of seven red giant members in the globular cluster Tononzintla 2. We used the APOGEE-2 near-infrared spectra to examine the abundance levels of multiple chemical species in these stars. The findings showed a moderate metal content and the absence of an internal variation in metal abundance. Tononzintla 2 exhibits an increased presence of alpha-enrichment which aligns with patterns observed in other rich-metallic galactic clusters. A nitrogen spread was discovered in Tononzintla 2 with multiple nitrogen-rich stars residing within it, indicating a nitrogen concentration in this cluster that surpasses average levels observed in multiple other rich-metallic galactic clusters, thus classifying it as a cluster with extreme nitrogen. A [Ce/Fe] spread was discovered and found to correlate with the nitrogen variation, suggesting a possible connection between the celeium anomaly and the nitrogen spread present in this cluster.

Formally verifying theorems in mathematics and computer science involves checking the soundness and completeness of theoretical foundations, which can be intricate and volatile. A powerful tool for this task is the Isabelle proof assistant, widely utilized for complex proofs by leading researchers. Although it has numerous advantages, one significant benefit stands out - the vast Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs (AFP), comprising over 900 formal proofs covering a broad range of topics. Our research focuses on the Isabelle theorem verification process and the AFP. We've developed a framework called TVF, which can assess and enhance the robustness of theorems in the archive. Additionally, we've employed TVF to create a reliable version of the AFP, dubbed TVP. This enhanced archive not only ensures the correctness of its contents but has also inspired new features, such as trustworthy versions of popular Isabelle libraries, which can be used in theorem verification projects.

Using the functional renormalization group, we have analyzed the Yang-Lee edge singularities near critical transitions for both scalar O(N) universality classes and the Ising universality class in quantum systems. By determining the position of the edge singularity, we found that it resides at $z= d/2$ on the critical line for all classical O(N) universality classes, with $d$ being the spatial dimension. This means that the edge singularity is located at $z = d/2 = 4/2 = 2$ when $d = 2$, and it does not exhibit universality. Additionally, we found that the edge singularity's position can be expressed as $z = d/2$ for all quantum systems we examined, with $z = 1/2$ when $d = 2$. Our analysis also enabled us to obtain the leading singular part of the susceptibility near the edge singularity, with specific values for $z = d/2 = 2$ and $z = 1/2$.

In statistical mechanics, researchers use the concept of variational principle to find upper and lower bounds for the model's free energy and establish the stability of its stationary points. Two powerful tools for this purpose are the replica method and the cavity approach, which can be utilized to analyze and bound the model's thermodynamic properties. The stochastic stability of a given minimum-free-energy solution can be determined by analyzing the second-order derivatives of the estimated free-energy function. Although the replica and cavity approaches provide insights into the model's thermodynamics, they do not directly facilitate the analysis of stochastic stability. The paper employs the stochastic TAP equation and its associated Feynman-Hibert decay estimator to investigate the stochastic stability of a model's minimum-free-energy solution. The stochastic TAP equation can be viewed as a perturbed version of the stochastic dynamics that arises from the application of the cavity and replica methods. The paper establishes a non-convexity property of the estimated TAP free energy, which is crucial for ensuring the stability of a model's minimum-free-energy solution. Additionally, the paper provides a novel proof of the local concavity of the estimated TAP free energy near its stable fixed points. The paper's results provide a general framework for addressing the stochastic stability of a model's minimum-free-energy solution, which can be applied to a wide range of disordered statistical mechanical models.

Recent advancements in nanotechnology and electromagnetic theory have enabled the design of controllable electromagnetic fields through spatially localized concepts, specifically quasi-conjugate surface interactions. This research focuses on the interface between a perfect electric conductor and a planar perfect magnetic conductor, which it applies to develop complex electromagnetic field control systems, leveraging microwave circuit components and microfluidic channels to create dynamic systems. A symbolic mathematical approach is proposed for complex field analysis, involving the expansion of electromagnetic wave expressions in terms of plane waves and generalized scattering matrices. Furthermore, this proposal can be extended to study non-conductive metasurfaces, represented by generalized conformal space transformation, and it demonstrates the potential to model various surface configurations using conformal transformations, ultimately enabling the analysis of complex field behavior in conformal surfaces.

The primary objective of this research is to validate the smooth local orbital linearization theorem for smooth fully integrable vector fields near a compact subset of a smooth manifold. Our proof leverages Ruh's approach, along with additional arguments. We also demonstrate that fully integrable vector fields exhibit key properties, including local stability and global smooth conjugacy to a linear conjugacy. Additionally, we provide an example illustrating that convergent smooth flows are not necessarily fully integrable.

This paper presents a deep learning approach called the Configuration Interaction Generator Network (CIGR), which generates the full potential energy surface (PES) from a set of one-electron interactions. The CIGR model utilizes a stacked neural network to accurately describe the complex relationships between electrons in a multi-electron system. When trained on a comprehensive dataset of configurations, it can effectively predict the potential energy, electron density, and other key properties for any electron configuration within that system. The CIGR model surpasses traditional configuration interaction methods in efficiency, making it a suitable candidate to guide the search for minimum energy configurations in high-dimensional electron correlation spaces. Moreover, this deep learning model can be applied across various domains of physics, including nuclear physics and chemistry.

A remarkable radio arc, dubbed Giant Structure FR-II (GSFR), has been lying undetected for centuries in the sky. Spanning an enormous 1.5 billion light-years, it creates a massive curved feature in the radio sky that was missing from cosmological simulations. The discovery of this massive structure in the sky was made possible by using data from the Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI). It exhibits distinct characteristics, including extended components that defy explanation and a peculiar alignment with the cosmic web. The duration it took to observe this feature in the sky was 30 years, from 1989 to 2019. The name Giant Structure FR-II is assigned to it. The designation starts with GSFR J0208+16, and it is also referred to as the Structure of GSFR. The name Giant Structure FR-II is assigned to it. The designation starts with GSFR J0208+16, and it is also referred to as the Structure of GSFR.

The use of photometry from low-cost cameras pointed at the sky for tracking atmospheric conditions has seen a significant surge in interest recently. This surge is driven by growing mobility and data storage capabilities, enabling vast amounts of data to be collected over expansive areas. However, the conventional method of measuring atmospheric parameters using the stellar extinction method has some major limitations, given the high level of variability in photometric quality. Nevertheless, our research has shown that even high-quality data can provide precise and accurate measurements of aerosol density in the atmosphere, using a method that takes into consideration the scattering of light by calculating the Rayleigh-Kruger parameter.

We are addressing a critical challenge in pose estimation research: posing an object based on an image. Current methods primarily rely on deep learning techniques, leveraging features from convolutional neural networks, but often overlook essential image properties. In contrast, we integrate projective groupings and correspondence learning into a single framework called DeepHMap++, which leverages both shallow and deep descriptors of images. Specifically, we utilize the fundamental matrix to represent correspondences and develop a novel algorithm called Progressive Grouping (PG) to identify projective gridding. PG is efficient, accurate, and versatile enough to be learned from training datasets. We employed a diverse set of benchmark datasets to evaluate our deep learning approach, and our results demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques in both accuracy and efficiency.

Peridynamic theories have seen a significant surge in adoption across various disciplines of engineering and physics to analyze complex problems characterized by abrupt failures and material discontinuities. This review distills the bond-based peridynamic approach into fundamental concepts, focusing on the mathematical framework, existence and uniqueness of solutions, and numerical implementation. Key applications spanning mechanics, materials science, and engineering have been extensively explored and represented through an extensive catalog of bond-based peridynamic problems. Furthermore, this review addresses the possibilities of extending the bond-based model to represent non-classical fluid dynamics, incorporating concepts of strain-driven fracture in fluid media and peridynamic fluids analyzed through numerical simulations.

We present GGLasso, a Python-based library designed to address Generalized Graphical Lasso (GGL) problems. Based on the PySparse matrix storage and operation framework, GGLasso offers an efficient and scalable solution for several types of generalized graphical lasso objectives, including those associated with multivariate linear models, sparse inverse additive models, and multi-task learning with sparse inverse matrices. The library takes advantage of PySparse's flexible memory management, allowing for straightforward implementation of update rules using autodifferentiated memory access, as demonstrated by the inclusion of both fixed-point and quasi-Newton methods in the library. As a result of its flexible storage and operation design, GGLasso is highly adaptable and capable of handling a variety of generalizations of the graphical lasso objective.

A newly proposed method for biasing Langevin dynamics towards preferred configurations has been presented, aiming to enhance the efficiency of biased simulations. The method effectively mitigates the bias-induced fluctuations during exploration, ensuring that the probability distribution of visited configurations accurately reflects the intended target. This approach has been found particularly beneficial for biased simulations focused on maintaining stable intermediate states, such as those involved in barrier-crossing events. The proposed method has been found to enhance the success rate of such simulations, compared to conventional techniques.

We conducted a series of simulations to examine how simulations of black hole collisions are affected by the properties of a cosmological fluid known as wave dark energy. We based our simulations on two popular models of wave dark energy, known as the quintessence model and the phantom model, and we determined the parameters of these models to be $\beta=0.5$ and $\alpha=0.2$ respectively. We utilized these simulations to study how collisions between black holes of $1.5M_\odot$ mass and black holes of $10M_\odot$ mass affect the behavior of wave dark energy. We found that in the quintessence model, the density of wave dark energy becomes less dense over time, whereas in the phantom model, the density of wave dark energy becomes more dense. We found that in the quintessence model, the energy released by the collision is reduced by a factor of approximately two as a result of the effects of wave dark energy, whereas in the phantom model, the energy released is increased by a factor of approximately two. We found that in the quintessence model, the amplitude of gravitational waves is reduced by a factor of approximately two as a result of the effects of wave dark energy, whereas in the phantom model, the amplitude is increased by a factor of approximately two. We found that in the quintessence model, the frequency of gravitational waves is shifted by a factor of approximately one as a result of the effects of wave dark energy,

We investigate the stability of an Euler-Bernoulli beam, specifically its elongated form, which is suspended between two points on a star-shaped graph. Determining the conditions for this configuration to be asymptotically stable is our primary objective. To approach this, we first establish a bridge between the given spatial dynamics and a related closed-loop system. By leveraging a Lyapunov function tailored to the connected graph, we obtain the required stability metric. Additionally, we explore the effects of the connectivity rate on the stability of the system.

Our novel acoustic lens substance, which we refer to as a metasurface lens with tapered holes, effectively increases the sensitivity of our photoacoustic detector by multiplying the detection area of the sensor by tenfold. Despite being incredibly thin, this lens offers high photoacoustic signal-to-noise ratio and precise image resolution, outperforming conventional lenses. It has been successfully applied to photoacoustic breast tomography, capable of detecting very small lesions with low power laser, and has been demonstrated using a phantom and actual human data.

A node's significance within a multilayer network is influenced by various factors, including the characteristics of individual layers and a node's connections to others. Our research focuses on identifying second-order importance measurements, or eigenvector prominence, that can highlight crucial components in multilayer networks by amplifying the inherent structure and suppressing superficial connections. We have developed an iterative approach to calculate this new metric and demonstrated its effectiveness in distinguishing latent community structures within multilayer networks, particularly those with loosely connected modules.

We tackle the issue of non-blind deblurring, demosaicking and denoising raw images using a novel approach that leverages a collaborative learning method between two models. Our strategy involves creating two models: one processes the demosaicked image and another works directly with the raw data. To ensure these models work well together, we employ a joint training method that minimizes the discrepancy between their outputs. We show that these models can achieve superior performance in various tasks, including deblurring, demosaicking and denoising, when they are optimized for raw images. Our methods also outperform state-of-the-art techniques in experiments.

Recently, we generated the $R$-Poincar\'e algebra using deformed Poisson brackets, 
which effectively replicate the Fock coordinate transformation. This transformation 
corresponds to a de Sitter spacetime. In this study, we formulate the Dirac equation within 
$R$-Minkowski spacetime and establish that it is analogous to the Dirac equation defined 
within the de Sitter spacetime, described by its conformally flat metric. We then propose 
a novel strategy to solve the Dirac equation within the de Sitter spacetime by adopting 
the Schr\"{o}dinger picture.

Intelligent systems that interact with humans or their environments often experience changes that influence future states, yet the underlying causal relationships between these entities remain unclear. To facilitate a more sophisticated and adaptive interaction, it's essential to identify these causal connections. The Causal Exploration Toolbox is a collection of proven methods for uncovering causal relationships, developed through interventions in Python. This framework addresses two pivotal challenges in causal discovery: the exploratory phase is rewarded for maximizing information gain while minimizing the cost of actions, and the exponential growth of potential connections makes them difficult to model. The Causal Exploration Toolbox is an open-source project available on GitHub.

Our research investigated the seal characteristics of spheres entering a liquid at moderate approach speeds, focusing on the regime between Stokes flow and fully turbulent flow. Previous studies of sphere entry into liquid were reviewed, and the limitations of existing work identified. We studied the seal surface formation around spheres entering a liquid at speeds from 0 to 75 cm/s, using high-speed cameras and particle image velocimetry. The results showed that the seal surface formed in an unstable manner in all flow regimes, contradicting the widely held assumption that it becomes stable in turbulent flow. Additionally, the dynamics of the seal surface were found to depend on both flow speed and fluid viscosity.

We investigate a comprehensive set of $\alpha'$-corrected Type IIB effective field theories, considering both extended quantum gravity descriptions and holographic dualities. Focusing on a toroidally-compactified four-dimensional framework, we explore the impact of higher-order $\alpha'$ corrections on a consistent effective theory. It is demonstrated that the extended quantum gravity theory, characterized by an infinite number of $\alpha'$-expanded Chern-Simons terms, incorporates the capabilities of higher-order gravitational transformations. Furthermore, we establish that the corrected effective action, including $\alpha'$-expanded gravitationally coupled Yang-Mills and scalar sectors, must adhere to specific constraints in order to ensure the consistency of the theory up to the next-to-next-to-leading order.

Cloud-based services provide convenient access to computer resources, but leveraging these services from home poses a risk due to potentially malicious household radio frequency emissions affecting hardware behavior, potentially introducing security vulnerabilities into the cloud. This threat could be mitigated if hardware used for connecting to the cloud is isolated from other electronic devices at home. However, this restriction would impose additional requirements on energy and real-time minimization problems, potentially limiting the choice of computationally feasible algorithms. This paper addresses this challenge by introducing a new minimization problem, minimizing confidence in energy and real-time predictions, and showcases its application to a case study involving heating control. A confidence measure is defined and subsequently minimized to balance the risk of malicious interference affecting hardware behavior and the computational efficiency of the optimization process. The proposed method is tested and compared with alternative strategies in a simulated environment.

Reinforcement learning (RL) is commonly used to optimize complex systems, but these systems can be vulnerable to cyber attacks that manipulate their decision-making processes. This research focuses on defending RL policies against sophisticated attacks that alter the data used for training, specifically those aimed at a particular critical state action. We are able to combat such attacks by leveraging an attack-resistant policy gradient, which is based on the concept that an attacker cannot prevent a RL agent from learning the expected rewards associated with different state actions. We validate our approach by simulating a critical state attack on a power grid system and show that it can be highly effective in defending the system against such attacks, allowing the system to function normally despite the corruption.

We've developed an intriguing paradox using an variant of the famous box game thought experiment, one that doesn't rely on selection. This thought experiment, similar to the original, results in a paradoxical outcome, challenging the principle of locality and the concept of free will. Our variation maintains the paradoxical nature of the outcome while avoiding the need for the principle of compositionality. This has significant implications for the free will theorem, suggesting that it's the compositionality aspect, rather than free will itself, that's being tested. Our theorem still holds true in a world without free will, as long as compositionality is present. This has further implications for the local hidden variable theories, implying that they must either grant free will or reject compositionality.

We examine the intriguing orbital selection phenomenon in cupricite CuFe2S3, where the crystal-field splitting of one iron orbital is unusually disrupted, shifting from the standard framework. Our study combines X-ray absorption near its edge, electron spin resonance, and theoretical modeling to delve into the local atomic behavior. The results reveal that the chosen orientation of cupricite's hexagonal channels forces the distorted iron octahedron to tilt, contributing to the observed orbital splitting anomaly. This understanding offers a remedy for the anticipated electronic instability in this material, potentially enabling better detection of the predicted orbital localization.

A promising approach to enhancing the vision of nanoscale science and the field of nanophotonics involves the synergistic development of quantum chemistry and quantum optics. We've achieved a breakthrough in this area by exhibiting enormous, over-pi Rabi oscillations between a highly localized, exciton state and a quasi-free, wave-like state without the need for an external magnetic field. This accomplishment was made possible by designing a specifically tailored, two-dimensional microcavity system in a way that its spatial structure harmoniously accommodates both the exciton's confined, atomic-like nature and the wave-like properties of light. Furthermore, our measurements demonstrate rapid, controllable switching between these two states, revealing a vast, exciton-related quantum fluctuation that causes a sudden, massive shift in the system's symmetry. This complex system also exhibits rare phenomena of multi-state interference and light-induced chemical reactions.

Our investigation reveals a 2D, lattice-based wallpaper structure that harbors an adjustable Dirac point within a non-symmorphic symmetry framework, specifically within the D6m group. 

We have mathematically demonstrated the existence of a unique, adjustable Dirac point within this lattice, where the point's location can be precisely controlled over an equilateral triangle area through adjustment of the lattice's interatomic distance.
 

Our study showcases that this adjustable Dirac point maintains singular, quasi Dirac states within the D6m group, characterized by minimal gaps of ~0.15eV, and high v2D values up to 10, along various SNAP directions.
 

We have derived the feasible extraction of massless, quasi Dirac fermions around this point by applying suitable on-site potentials, resulting in the separation of systems into two distinct sub-layers with contrasting Dirac states.
 

Our study also derives the feasible creation of stable, massless quasi Dirac states along the SNAP directions on honeycomb structures, achievable through on-site potential adjustments, potentially enabling the exploration of novel physics associated with massless Dirac fermions in 2D systems.

We examine a system consisting of an atom and a cavity, interacting with a multi-photon input field with the purpose of creating a single-photon facilitated coherent state output field. A unitary transformation is applied to the system and the cavity field is analyzed in two scenarios: with and without the multi-photon input field. Quantum optical catalysis is used to achieve an approximate single-photon transformation of a coherent state. A applied field can aid in obtaining a facilitated coherent state. These outcomes occur even when the multi-photon input field is not entangled with the system. A quantum metrology application is proposed to detect fuel enanglement. A proposed experiment includes an atom interacting with a cavity, coupled to a triphoton source, and demonstrates the creation of a single-photon facilitated coherent state. A calculation of the state reconstruction from homodyne data is also presented.

In General Relativity using the Newman-Penrose formalism, a key component is a bivector, which is analogous to an electromagnetic field vector in the standard Minkowski space. This paper delves into the specifics of bivector calculus within the Newman-Penrose formalism and explores its application to electromagnetism and conformal curvature constructs in General Relativity. We demonstrate that the conventional Maxwell equations and the Ricci matrix are inherent consequences of the conformal curvature matrix equation, known as the Bondi-Gel'fand equation. Furthermore, we define a specific matrix operator that transforms electromagnetism in the standard Minkowski space in a linear fashion. This operator maintains the same form when changing from the standard Minkowski space to the complex null tetrad space used in the Newman-Penrose formalism. We also introduce a new formalism, referred to as the Weyl curvature matrix formalism, which separates the conformal curvature matrix into distinct pure matrix components. This results in a simplified formulation of conformal curvature constructs in General Relativity, allowing for a direct comparison with the standard formulation using the Newman-Penrose formalism.

A novel technique has been introduced for creating random integer models by using linear regression and mixed-integer linear programming. This technique involves generating a linear regression model to predict target values, transforming those predictions into the desired range, and then developing a mixed-integer linear programming model to accurately estimate a discrete version of the target. We have applied this technique to create Monte Carlo test cases with specific distributional characteristics in various dimensions. Furthermore, we have utilized our derived models to examine the performance of optimization algorithms, specifically focusing on the impact of increasing problem size on solution time.

Optimizing the performance of control systems in continuous processes relies heavily on the use of numerical methods for solving parametric problems, such as optimizing, identifying, and solving model-based control systems. This involves setting up a problem in the form of a parameter optimization problem, transforming it into a set of ordinary differential equations through direct transcription methods, and then solving it using suitable numerical integration methods. This approach offers several advantages over traditional methods based on the method of characteristics, such as the ability to incorporate constraints, differentiate complex functions, and integrate control and estimation methods directly. This tutorial provides a comprehensive overview of the direct transcription method and highlights its key features, along with a case study on a dual-patient breathing system during the COVID-19 pandemic, where the rapid spread of the virus has caused hospitals to be overwhelmed with patients in need of life-supporting ventilator treatment. The resulting code is then applied to a coarsedistributed computing framework, where it demonstrates significant improvements in performance, reducing the computational time by up to 90%.

A cutting-edge new method has been presented for automatically identifying and outlining neoplasms in the esophagus using CT scans. A innovative technique was proposed by our team to develop an medical imaging algorithm. This technique involved an innovative attention-based model that combined dense connections and constricted dense layers to control data entry, ensuring that only crucial information from various image slices is considered when predicting boundaries. We utilized very detailed training datasets consisting of 4000 data sets of CT scans with neoplasms, collected from two major sources. Neoplasms in these scans appear as irregularly shaped white masses. Our proposed algorithm was capable of accurately outlining these masses in just one pass over the data, without needing information about their actual shape. We compared the performance of our algorithm to several established methods by applying it to a large test dataset of 7000 data sets. Our proposed algorithm consistently produced the most accurate results in all trials, outperforming even a model that had access to actual images of neoplasms.
